title: Extending the mean first-passage-time formalism to the reconstruction of high free-energy barriers: A top-start approach
abstract: Rare events, such as crystal nucleation in mildly supercooled liquids, are characterized by waiting times that can be much longer than the timescale of the underlying microscopic dynamics. The mean first-passage time (MFPT) formalism [J. Wedekind and D. Reguera, J. Phys. Chem. B 112, 11060 (2008)] provides a route to reconstruct one-dimensional free-energy profiles from the MFPT and steady-state distribution measured along a reaction coordinate, but conventional implementations become inefficient for sufficiently high barriers because spontaneous crossings are rarely observed. We introduce a "top-start" extension that initiates trajectories near the barrier top and reconstructs the free-energy profile from their subsequent evolution away from the barrier toward lower-free-energy regions. We establish the equivalence between the top-start and two-region constructions using a Markov-chain transition-matrix formulation. We validate the method using one-dimensional random-walk simulations across low, medium, and high free-energy barriers, with transition-matrix calculations providing an exact benchmark for the corresponding discretized models. The top-start reconstruction remains accurate in the high-barrier regime where conventional MFPT sampling becomes prohibitively inefficient.
summary: This work extends the Mean First-Passage Time (MFPT) formalism to reliably reconstruct free-energy profiles across very high barriers. It introduces a "top-start" sampling technique that overcomes the inefficiency of waiting for rare spontaneous crossings. This method is validated using random-walk simulations and confirms its accuracy where conventional sampling fails.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of reconstructing high free-energy barriers from Mean First-Passage Time (MFPT) data, a task made computationally prohibitive by the rarity of spontaneous barrier crossings.
main_result: A novel "top-start" extension to the MFPT formalism is introduced, which accurately reconstructs free-energy profiles even in the high-barrier regime by initiating trajectories near the barrier top.
method: The method leverages Markov-chain transition-matrix formulations to establish the equivalence between the top-start approach and conventional two-region constructions for calculating MFPTs and free-energy profiles.
model_or_system: The model involves a particle undergoing Brownian motion along a one-dimensional potential landscape, which is discretized and treated as a Markov process. The dynamics are governed by the Fokker-Planck equation in the continuous limit.
key_observables: Mean first-passage time ($	au(x)$), steady-state distribution ($P_{st}(x)$), and the reconstructed free-energy profile ($ eta U(x)$).
important_parameters: The analysis covers low, medium, and high free-energy barrier regimes, with the inverse temperature $ eta = 1/(k_B T)$ being a key parameter.
main_assumptions: The dynamics are assumed to be Markovian, and the reconstruction relies on the established relationships between MFPT, steady-state flux, and the potential energy landscape.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the decomposition of a top-start trajectory into region-restricted paths for different sides of a barrier, confirming the equivalence between the simulation method and theoretical region-specific calculations.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical basis using MFPT and steady-state flux relations, then introduces the top-start sampling technique, and finally validates this method using random-walk simulations across varying barrier heights.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the rigorous mathematical framework for rare event sampling and barrier crossing dynamics is foundational to understanding non-equilibrium processes in complex quantum systems, such as quantum tunneling rates or reaction rates in open quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Schematic representation of regions A and B relative to the common reflecting and initial position a = x0. Region A extends from a toward the absorbing boundary b1 < a and carries a steady-state flux JA < 0, whereas region B extends from a toward the absorbing boundary b2 > a and carries a steady-state flux JB > 0. The position a need not coincide with the free-energy maximum.

FIG. 2: Model double-well potentials used in the RW simulations for the low-, medium-, and high-barrier cases. The corresponding barrier heights, measured from the left-well minimum, are approximately 2, 8, and 20kBT, respectively.

FIG. 3: Conventional MFPT reconstruction for the low- and medium-barrier model potentials. The first and second rows correspond to the low- and medium-barrier cases, respectively. From left to right, the columns show Pst(x), −lnPst(x), the MFPT τ(x), and the reconstructed free-energy profile βU(x). All the RW results are compared with TM calculations, while the reconstructed free-energy profiles are compared with the corresponding model potentials.

FIG. 4: Two-region reconstruction for the low-, medium-, and high-barrier model potentials. The rows correspond to increasing barrier height. From left to right, the columns show the region-specific steady-state distributions PA st(x) and PB st(x), the corresponding MFPTs τA(x) and τB(x), and the reconstructed free-energy profile βU(x). All the RW results are compared with TM calculations. In the free-energy panels, the model potential is compared with reconstructions obtained from the RW and TM quantities for regions A and B.

FIG. 5: Top-start reconstruction for the low-, medium-, and high-barrier model potentials. The rows correspond to increasing barrier height. From left to right, the columns show the region-specific steady-state distributions PA st(x) and PB st(x), the corresponding MFPTs τA(x) and τB(x), and the reconstructed free-energy profile βU(x). The steady-state distributions and MFPTs obtained from the top-start RW trajectories are compared with TM calculations, while the reconstructed free-energy profiles are compared directly with the corresponding model potentials.
